items.rule: Do not pre-emptively add useCallback, useMemo, or similar React optimizations unless there is a concrete stability/performance requirement (e.g. dependency of another memoized value, debounced handler identity, memoized child boundary, effect cleanup identity). Prefer plain functions by default.

Do not propose or use formatting/inlining tricks to reduce CodeScene LOC/complexity in Prettier-managed code. Prefer meaningful extractions into functions outside the main function, especially when addressing CodeScene complex-method issues.

During review-comment triage, keep analysis scoped to the reviewed code unless the user explicitly asks for broader context. Do not include a 'same issue elsewhere' or wider-audit suggestion by default.

When triaging code review comments, be more critical: compare the suggested change against pre-branch/origin behavior and the PR goal before marking it warranted. A suggestion that improves behavior can still be not warranted if it introduces new behavior outside the PR's intended compatibility scope.

Do not write unnecessary tests or tests for the sake of coverage. Write tests intentionally around meaningful feature behavior and user-observable outcomes. Avoid tests that only lock down tiny implementation details, incidental markup/absence, or every small code change; such tests become maintenance hurdles without protecting real behavior.

In hs-web-app under pi, Volta yarn shims can fail because pi sets _VOLTA_TOOL_RECURSION=1. Run Node/Yarn commands as `env -u _VOLTA_TOOL_RECURSION yarn ...` so Volta can resolve the project-pinned Node/Yarn.

When using the dissect-plan skill, the output should be a revised plan after discussion, not immediate implementation. Do not implement a dissected plan unless the user separately approves implementation.

Do not let the current working directory determine the target for a change. First infer and confirm the user's intent and the runtime/application surface. For pi extension tweaks, default to the auto-discovered applied extension locations (`~/.pi/agent/extensions/` or `.pi/extensions/`) because those are what `/reload` loads; treat sync repos as copies unless explicitly asked to sync them.

Always take things step by step. Diagnose/explain first, then propose options and brainstorm with the user before implementing. Never build or fix anything without explicit approval. If the user wants to offload everything, they will say so explicitly.

Do not anchor workflow decisions on exact trigger words. Infer the user's intent from the whole context, task framing, prior discussion, and whether a concrete implementation has been approved. If intent is investigative/review/planning, stay non-mutating and report findings. If intent clearly delegates execution of a concrete change, proceed. When uncertain, ask a short confirmation before mutating.

When creating or updating a user-authored pi skill in ~/.pi/agent/skills, also sync it into ~/pi-config-sync: copy the skill folder, update extensions/pi-config-sync/index.ts MANAGED_SKILL_DIRS, and update pi-config-sync.manifest.json managedFiles/managedRoots unless the user explicitly says not to sync it.

Do not test or rely on a just-edited pi extension tool in the same session by calling the registered tool unless its runtime implementation has been verified active. File diffs can show new code while the loaded tool remains old; use /reload/new session and verify behavior, or avoid the tool.

In pi-config-sync, do not add or modify user-authored skills without checking all skill sync invariants: local ~/.pi/agent/skills/*, repo skills/*, extensions/pi-config-sync MANAGED_SKILL_DIRS, and pi-config-sync.manifest.json managedFiles/managedRoots must agree. Run an explicit inventory check before saying skill sync is complete.

Do not lead the user into a false binary or over-constrained solution space. When debugging races or async flows, explicitly consider simple sequencing fixes that preserve all required side effects (e.g. eager synchronous state alignment before async execution) before suggesting larger guard/suppression mechanisms. If an option may be incomplete or risky, state uncertainty and ask to validate rather than presenting it as the main path.

Do not treat naming-direction or design-preference discussion as implementation approval. When the user says a name/API "should" reflect something or asks whether a rename is warranted, first propose options and wait for explicit selection/approval before editing files. Positive wording about a direction is not approval of a specific name or implementation.

Do not create issue-tracker artifacts during Wayfinder charting until the user explicitly approves the concrete map and ticket set and asks for issue creation. Approval of planning direction is not approval to mutate the tracker.

When the user responds positively to a proposed implementation plan with phrases like 'that sounds reasonable', infer approval to implement unless they explicitly say not to write code or ask only for more discussion.

When implementing an agreed task, do not introduce incidental refactors or parameter-shape/API changes just to satisfy tooling without first informing the user. Stick to the approved scope; if tooling or design concerns arise, pause and raise the issue with options, or make the minimal requested change and explicitly report any unresolved concerns.

When the user asks a specific verification question, do not answer confidently unless verified. State uncertainty explicitly. If prior observed behavior contradicts the claim, trust the observation and do not repeat the action.

During grill-me/design questioning, do not continue down a branch after the user's prior answer has already resolved it. Reconcile each new question against established decisions first, and if a question is invalid under those decisions, state that and move on instead of leading the user toward a contradictory design.
In hs-web-app Wayfinder work, do not call the completed map or ticket resolutions "specs"; refer to them as the planning map, implementation guidance, or resolved decisions.
When branch state is relevant, re-run `git branch --show-current` immediately before claiming the user is still on a branch; do not rely on an earlier check after the user may have switched branches.

When creating or updating general pi skills for the user, write them to the user's local pi config under ~/.pi/agent/skills/ by default, not to the current project's .agents/skills or AGENTS.md, unless the user explicitly asks for a project-local skill.

Do not wait for magic words like "implement" in every case, but distinguish approval from exploration by context: infer implementation approval only when there is a concrete proposed action/plan/name/API already on the table and the user affirmatively accepts it. If the user is still shaping criteria, expressing preferences, or adding constraints without selecting a concrete option, continue discussion and ask/propose before editing.

When working on pi extensions from ~/pi-config-sync, do not edit the sync repo as the runtime source by default. First identify and confirm the local/applied extension path, edit that path for behavior changes, and only update pi-config-sync intentionally when the user asks to sync/persist/distribute the change.

Do not default to shortcut or symptom-treating fixes. Prefer fixing the actual root cause. If suggesting a shortcut/workaround, explicitly label it as a tradeoff/caveat and explain why it is not the root-cause fix.

Never infer authorization for external mutations from general workflow approval. Content approval, planning approval, "proceed," skill invocation, existing labels, authentication, or prior external usage do not authorize creating or modifying GitHub issues, Jira tickets, PRs, comments, remote branches, uploads, or any other external artifact. Default to local work and obtain explicit permission for the exact external write immediately beforehand.
Do not implement scaffolding, component APIs, files, or inferred UI beyond the exact action the user explicitly approved. If the user asks to create only a folder, create only the folder and stop.

When the user asks to review their latest code changes, do not make unsolicited edits or revert their choices. First inspect current files/diff, then report issues only if there are real problems. If an edit is needed, ask or limit changes to exactly what the user requested.
